blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A census measures every unit in the population. A sample survey measures a subset and uses it to estimate the population’s values. Sampling is chosen over a census for cost, time and feasibility, and sometimes because the measurement itself destroys or uses up the unit.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Why not always measure everyone? Because a census takes far more time, staff and money, and by the time it is finished the situation it measured may have changed. Some measurements also cannot be taken on every unit without destroying the population itself. A sample is not only cheaper. Because it needs far fewer field staff, those staff can be better trained and supervised, so errors in data collection can be smaller than in a census.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Testing the potency of every vaccine vial in a batch would use up the whole batch: sampling is the only option that leaves any vaccine to give. At the other extreme, a population census is so large that its quality is itself checked by a sample. A sub-sample is re-enumerated “by using better trained and more experienced staff than those employed for the main investigation” (Banda, 2003).

points.html: A well-designed sample can match, and sometimes beat, a census in accuracy, because a census carries large non-sampling errors (coverage, response and recording errors, §6.4) that a smaller, better-supervised survey can reduce.
“Well-designed” is the crucial qualifier. The rest of this chapter is about what makes a design good.
